lessons.title: This week's storylines
lessons.objective: Explain what is being discussed in hockey right now.

payload.prompt: Match each weekly-storyline term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A player or team winning or scoring far above normal for a stretch.
A stretch where a good player or team stops scoring or winning.
An injury expected to keep a player out only briefly.
Having played one fewer game than a rival in the standings.

explanation.summary: These four phrases turn up in almost every weekly hockey chat. Hot and cold streaks, injuries and games in hand are the storylines behind most of the headlines.
explanation.sayThisLine: So what's the big story in hockey this week?

payload.prompt: A player with 6 goals in the last five games is in a slump.

scene.alt: A player has scored 6 goals recently.

explanation.correct: False. Six goals in five games is a hot streak. A slump is when a scorer goes cold, and fans notice both.
explanation.incorrect: That pace is a hot streak, which is a storyline of its own. A slump is the opposite: a scorer who has gone quiet.

statement.speaker: Riley
statement.text: Our top line is on fire right now. Twelve points between them in three games.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: Her team's best players have been scoring a lot lately.
options.explanation: Right. 'On fire' means playing great, and that many points in three games is a hot stretch.

options.text: The arena is literally on fire.
options.explanation: It is hockey talk, not an emergency. She means the players are scoring.

options.text: The top line always scores this much.
options.explanation: 'On fire' means better than usual. That is exactly why she mentioned it.

payload.translation: Her team's best line has been scoring at a great pace this week.

followUps.line: Is it helping them in the playoff race?
followUps.why: Connects a hot stretch to what it means for the season.

followUps.line: Who has been the best of the three?
followUps.why: Invites her to name names, which is what fans love to do.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Streaks and slumps are weekly talking points. Ask her what she has noticed.

payload.prompt: Complete the fan line about injuries.
payload.template: 'Day-to-day' means a player is expected to miss {{short}}, while LTIR is for players out {{long}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Day-to-day is a short, uncertain absence. LTIR, the long-term injured reserve, is how teams handle a player who will be out a long time.
explanation.incorrect: Day-to-day means a short absence, and LTIR is for long ones. When fans ask about an injury, the first question is usually how long.

lessons.title: Reading the standings today
lessons.objective: Interpret the live standings table and what {{team}}'s position means.

live.refreshHint: daily; hourly on game days late in the season

payload.prompt: Complete the NHL points line.
payload.template: An NHL team earns {{win}} points for any win and {{otl}} point for an overtime or shootout loss.

explanation.correct: Right. Every NHL win is worth two points, even in overtime or a shootout, and a loss after regulation still earns one. A regulation loss earns nothing.
explanation.incorrect: An NHL win is worth two points. A loss in overtime or a shootout earns one, and a loss inside 60 minutes earns none.

payload.prompt: A team has 70 points with 10 games left. Most points it can reach?

explanation.correct: Exactly 90. Ten wins at two points each adds 20 to the 70 they already have. Fans use this kind of math to see if a team can still catch the playoff line.
explanation.incorrect: The ceiling is every remaining game won: 10 games times 2 points is 20, and 70 plus 20 is 90.

payload.prompt: Two NHL teams are tied on points. What is the first tiebreaker?

options.text: Regulation wins.
Head-to-head record.
Alphabetical order.

explanation.correct: Yes. Regulation wins come first, which rewards winning inside 60 minutes. After that come regulation plus overtime wins and other measures.
explanation.incorrect: The first tiebreaker is regulation wins, then regulation plus overtime wins (ROW). Head-to-head is further down the list.

statement.speaker: Sarah
statement.text: We're five points out with a game in hand. We can still make the wild card.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Her team is five points behind a wild-card spot but has played one fewer game.
options.explanation: Right. 'Game in hand' means one fewer game played, so she has an extra chance to pick up points.

options.text: Her team has five extra games left.
options.explanation: 'Game in hand' means one fewer game played, not five extra games.

options.text: The wild card is decided by one game.
options.explanation: A game in hand is a standings advantage, not a deciding game.

payload.translation: They are five points behind the last playoff spot, but they have played one fewer game, so there is still a path.

followUps.line: How many games does your team have left?
followUps.why: Moves to the concrete math of how much time they have.

followUps.line: Who is holding that wild-card spot right now?
followUps.why: Shows you are tracking the race.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A game in hand is real but is not a guarantee. It only helps if they win it.

lessons.title: The playoff race
lessons.objective: Explain who is in, out and on the bubble in the NHL playoff push.

live.refreshHint: daily; hourly on game days late in the season

payload.prompt: How many wild-card teams per conference make the NHL playoffs?

options.text: One.
Two.
Three.

explanation.correct: Right. The top three teams in each division qualify, plus two wild cards per conference, for eight teams per conference and sixteen overall.
explanation.incorrect: It is two. Three per division plus two wild cards per conference gives eight per conference, sixteen in the playoffs.
explanation.sayThisLine: The wild card is the last playoff spot, going to the next-best record in the conference.

payload.prompt: Your team is two points out with 20 games left. What now?

situation.narrative: The team is on the playoff bubble with plenty of season left.

facts.label: Injuries
facts.value: Top center out two more weeks

options.label: Panic and trade for a rental right now.
options.consequence: Overreacting this early usually backfires. The team still has time to make up ground.

options.label: Give it ten more games, then reassess.
options.consequence: You learn whether the team can close the gap on its own, and the center is healthy again by then.
considerations: The deadline gives you time to add later.
The injury should heal by then.

options.label: Sell the veterans and plan for next year.
options.consequence: Selling while two points out gives up a real chance for not much in return.

payload.expertNote: Bubble teams often wait to see how the race develops before making a big move, and the deadline is the natural checkpoint.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: We're on the bubble. One bad week and we could fall out.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her team is close to the last playoff spot and a losing streak could end its chances.
options.explanation: Right. 'On the bubble' means right at the playoff line, in the race but vulnerable to a slide.

options.text: Her team is already eliminated.
options.explanation: The bubble is the opposite of eliminated. They are still in it, just barely.

options.text: Her team has clinched a playoff spot.
options.explanation: If they had clinched, they would be safe. The bubble means they are not safe yet.

payload.translation: Her team is sitting right at the playoff line. They are in the race, but a slide could knock them out.

followUps.line: How have they done in their last ten games?
followUps.why: Asks for the trend, which affects their chances.

followUps.line: Who else is fighting for that last spot?
followUps.why: Shows you are tracking the pack.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The bubble is stressful. Let her vent before you analyze it.

payload.prompt: Match each playoff-race term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Right at the playoff line, in the race but vulnerable to dropping out.
One of two playoff spots per conference for non-division-winners.
Too far behind to realistically make the playoffs.

explanation.summary: The playoff race has its own language: bubble, wild card and out. Use them and you will sound like you follow the race.
explanation.sayThisLine: Where does your team sit in the race right now?

lessons.title: Watching a live game
lessons.objective: Follow {{team}}'s game in progress and understand what matters.

payload.prompt: It is tied late in the third and your team takes a penalty. What matters most?

options.text: Killing the penalty without giving up the go-ahead goal.
Pulling the goalie for an extra attacker.
Waiting for the period to end so nothing counts.
Nothing. A tie game means penalties do not matter.

explanation.correct: Yes. A late tied game can be decided by one power-play goal, so the penalty kill is the whole story until it ends.
explanation.incorrect: Penalties always matter, and late in a tie they can decide the game. Pulling the goalie is for a team that is trailing.

payload.prompt: Your team gets a power play. What should you watch first?

options.text: Whether they get into the offensive zone cleanly.
Whether the goalie's glove hand looks tired.
How many hits are thrown.

explanation.correct: Yes. A power play starts with the zone entry. If they cannot carry the puck in cleanly they never get to set up, and that is a common reason power plays struggle.
explanation.incorrect: Watch the zone entry first. A power play that cannot get in cleanly never gets to run its setup.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: They scored, but we still have all the momentum.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Her team is outplaying the other team even though it is behind.
options.explanation: Right. Momentum is about who is controlling play, not the scoreboard. She expects her team to score next.

options.text: The other team's goal will not count.
options.explanation: A goal counts. She only means her team is playing better.

options.text: Her team is about to be awarded a goal.
options.explanation: Nobody is awarding anything. She is describing who has the feel of the game.

payload.translation: Her team is playing well and creating chances. One goal down does not mean they will lose.

followUps.why: Time left decides how much momentum can matter.

followUps.line: Are they getting good chances or just shots?
followUps.why: Helps tell whether the momentum is real.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Momentum is a feeling fans trust. Ask what she is seeing.

payload.prompt: It is 4-3 with 90 seconds left and {{team}} is down. They pull the goalie for an extra skater.

scene.alt: The goalie is off the ice and an extra attacker replaces him.

explanation.correct: Right. Down one with 90 seconds left, pulling the goalie is a normal gamble for the tie. An empty-net goal against costs little, since they are losing anyway.
explanation.incorrect: Down one late, pulling the goalie is standard. The risk is an empty-netter, but a one-goal loss and a two-goal loss count the same in the standings.

lessons.title: The hockey calendar
lessons.objective: Explain what happens each month and where the season is now.

payload.prompt: When does the NHL regular season usually start?

options.text: Early September.
Late September or early October.
November.

explanation.correct: Right. Preseason games come first, then the regular season opens in late September or early October and runs into April.
explanation.incorrect: The regular season opens in late September or early October. Preseason games come before it and do not count in the standings.

payload.prompt: Put the hockey year in order, starting with opening night.

items.text: Opening night of the regular season
items.why: The season starts in late September or early October.
Usually in the winter, with the regular season still running.
Runs into April, then the standings are set.
Held after the Final, usually in late June.
July 1, the day the big signings happen.

explanation.correct: Right. Opening night, the deadline, the end of the regular season, the playoffs, the draft and then free agency. Exact dates move a little each year.
explanation.incorrect: The order is opening night, deadline, regular season ends, playoffs, draft, then free agency on July 1.
explanation.sayThisLine: The deadline is when teams show whether they are buying or selling.

payload.prompt: Why is the trade deadline such a big day?

options.text: It is the last day teams can make trades, so contenders add rentals and sellers trade veterans for picks.
It marks the end of the regular season.
It is when the draft lottery is held.

explanation.correct: Yes. After the deadline, rosters are set for the stretch run. Contenders buy help for the playoffs and sellers trade veterans for picks and prospects.
explanation.incorrect: The deadline is the last chance to make trades for the season. It does not end the regular season or hold the lottery.

payload.prompt: Complete the line about the NHL Draft.
payload.template: The NHL Draft happens {{when}} and teams {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Right. The draft is usually held in late June, after the Cup Final, and teams pick young prospects to build their future.
explanation.incorrect: The draft comes after the season, in late June, and is where teams choose young prospects.

lessons.title: Trade deadline talk
lessons.objective: Explain why a trade at the deadline matters and the {{team}} strategy.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We got a rental: a winger on an expiring deal who leaves in July.

payload.question: What is he saying?

options.text: A player whose contract ends this summer, brought in for a playoff run.
options.explanation: Right. A rental is short-term help. The team gets a boost now, and the player becomes a free agent in the summer.

options.text: The team is renting an arena.
options.explanation: In trade talk, a rental is a player on an expiring contract.

options.text: The player will stay for a decade.
options.explanation: A rental leaves in the summer unless he re-signs.

payload.translation: A rental is a player on a deal that ends this year. The buying team pays in picks or prospects for a playoff boost.

followUps.line: What did they give up for him?
followUps.why: Moves to the cost of the trade.

followUps.line: Would they try to re-sign him?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rentals are a deadline staple. If you are lost, ask what they paid.

payload.prompt: Deadline day: your team is far from a playoff spot. What now?

situation.narrative: Your team is well outside the playoff picture with about 20 games left. Two key players have contracts that expire in July.

facts.label: Standings
facts.value: 10 points behind the last playoff spot

options.label: Trade the expiring players for picks and prospects.
options.consequence: You get real assets for players who would leave in July anyway.
considerations: Contenders pay more at the deadline.
You start building for next season.

options.label: Keep everyone and hope for a run.
options.consequence: It protects the current roster, but you risk losing both players for nothing.
considerations: A ten-point gap is hard to close.

options.label: Trade picks for a rental to push for the playoffs.
options.consequence: You spend future assets on a long shot.
considerations: Ten points back with 20 games left is a big hill.

payload.expertNote: Teams far out of the race usually sell players on expiring deals, because those players are leaving anyway.

payload.prompt: A player has a $6 million cap hit but earns $8 million. Why do teams care about the cap hit?

options.text: It is what counts against the salary cap.
It is the player's actual paycheck.
It is what the team wishes it could pay.

explanation.correct: Right. A cap hit is a contract's average annual value, which is what counts against the team's cap. It can differ from actual pay in any one year, and trades move that number between teams.
explanation.incorrect: The cap hit is the number the league's cap counts, which is not the same as what the player is paid that season.

payload.prompt: A rental is always the better deadline move than a long-term player.

scene.alt: Two players: one on a rental deal, one under contract long-term.

explanation.correct: False. It depends on the team. A contender chasing a title may love a rental, while a team building for the future would rather add a player who will stay.
explanation.incorrect: Rentals help contenders this season. Teams thinking long-term often prefer a player who will still be there next year.

lessons.title: Playoff mode
lessons.objective: Explain playoff intensity and what a series win means for {{team}}.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: It's Game 7 tomorrow. Winner take all.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The last game of a best-of-seven decides who moves on.
options.explanation: Right. Game 7 is the decider. Whoever wins advances and the loser is out.

options.text: Every series goes exactly seven games.
options.explanation: A series ends as soon as one team gets four wins. Game 7 only happens if it is 3-3.

options.text: It is a regular-season game.
options.explanation: Game 7 only exists in the playoffs.

payload.translation: It is the final, deciding game. The winner advances and the loser goes home.

followUps.why: Home ice is a big edge in a Game 7.
Invites the story of the series.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Game 7 is playoff folklore. Let her tell you her story.

payload.prompt: In a best-of-seven series, how many wins does a team need to advance?

options.text: Three.
Four.
Five.

explanation.correct: Right. First to four wins advances, and the series ends the moment one team gets there.
explanation.incorrect: It is four. The first team to win four games takes the series, even if that happens before game seven.

payload.prompt: In a best-of-seven, the team with home ice hosts Game 7.

scene.alt: A series schedule showing home games for each team.

explanation.correct: True. The team with home ice hosts Games 1, 2, 5 and 7, which is why fans fight so hard for it. It is a real advantage if the series goes the distance.
explanation.incorrect: Home ice means hosting Games 1, 2, 5 and 7, so the team with it gets the deciding game in its own building.

payload.prompt: Complete the playoff series facts.
payload.template: A team that leads a best-of-seven 3-1 needs {{wins}} more win to clinch, and a series tied 3-3 goes to {{game}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Four wins clinch a series, so a 3-1 lead is one win away, and 3-3 sends it to a deciding Game 7.
explanation.incorrect: A series is won with four wins. At 3-1 a team needs one more, and at 3-3 the seventh game decides it.
